# Role-Conditioned Refusals: Evaluating Access Control Reasoning in Large Language Models

## Research question

An otherwise answerable database request may be unauthorized for one role. The study asks whether language models can recognize that distinction while preserving useful SQL generation for permitted requests.

## Method

Spider and BIRD are converted to PostgreSQL and paired with four synthetic table/column permission profiles. The study compares direct SQL-or-refuse prompting, SQL generation followed by an LLM policy verifier, and Spider-trained LoRA models. Reference-query execution supplies artifact labels.

## Evaluation

Experiments report refusal precision/recall/F1, false permits and SQL execution accuracy, with policy-length and verifier-swap analyses. A separate OrgAccess classification test and a 2,000-instance retry-agent simulation extend evaluation. Fine-tuning reuses original Spider splits but reports a disjoint role-conditioned evaluation; released split membership was not audited.

## What the results support

Two-stage verification improves many zero-shot results, but not every few-shot comparison. LoRA refusal performance drops under Spider-to-BIRD transfer. Longer policies correlate with poorer results, and qualitative errors include refusal text followed by SQL. Permission-aware simulation reports fewer repeated calls.

## Limits and qualifications

These model judgments do not replace database enforcement or certify intrinsic answerability. Execution accuracy is discussed for correctly permitted requests, rather than unconditional success. Spider documentation maps all ERROR strings to DENY; BIRD documents privilege-specific filtering. Error-label purity, disjoint splits and published model runs were not independently verified.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

A distinct public policy-refusal benchmark and precursor to the collection's access-control probe study, useful for separating authorization, SQL correctness, over-refusal and genuinely unsupported questions.
